strengths: Timely and well-motivated research question: challenging the 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation is relevant to realistic, interactive deployments, and the paper clearly articulates why static evaluation may overestimate robustness.

The problem formalization (Section 3.1) is clean and general: the two-stage decomposition M(q)->(r_X) then M(q,r_X,i)->(r'_{X'},a') cleanly extends static accuracy to interruption-conditioned accuracy A_i(X) and length L_i(X), and naturally covers hard interrupts, soft speedup interrupts, and update-driven interrupts.

The empirical analysis identifies several concrete, well-documented failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) with quantitative characterization (e.g., up to 10x longer answers after hard interrupts, 30% accuracy drops under speedup, ~80% of update-driven errors attributable to self-doubt), supported by qualitative examples in Appendix C that convincingly illustrate the phenomena.

Reasonable experimental breadth: three model families (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, Magstral) plus scaling ablations (1.7B/8B/32B), four benchmarks across math and coding, multiple interrupt positions X in [0.1, 0.9], bootstrap confidence intervals, and assistant-turn vs. user-turn comparison.

The dataset construction process is documented in detail (Appendix D), including prompts, examples, and a multi-stage pipeline with manual verification; prompts for all experimental conditions are provided in Appendix B, and project page/code/dataset links are offered, supporting reproducibility.
Honest limitations section: the authors acknowledge restricted domains, single/well-defined interruptions, and a small model set, and do not overclaim generality beyond math/coding tasks.
The finding that 'thinking tokens vs. accuracy' compute plots understate real inference cost because of reasoning leakage is a genuinely useful correction to common evaluation practice.
weaknesses: Ground-truth correctness of the augmented (updated) problems is the central validity concern: updates are generated with GPT-5 and 'manually verified by the authors,' but the paper reports no inter-annotator agreement, error rates of the augmentation pipeline, or independent verification that a*(q,u) is correct. Errors here would directly contaminate the headline self-doubt and update-driven findings.

The model coverage is narrow (three ~open-weight reasoning models, all evaluated via a specific assistant-turn injection mechanism that some models handle poorly, as the authors themselves note for Qwen3/Magstral formatting). Claims about 'state-of-the-art LRMs' would be stronger with closed frontier models or more architectures.

Some headline numbers derive from very small evaluation sets: AIME 24/25 (30 problems x 16 trials) drives the 'up to 60%' degradation claim; variance is high and the paper does not always make per-dataset statistical significance clear.

The diagnosis of 'self-doubt' as the cause of ~80% of update-driven errors appears to rely on qualitative/behavioral categorization of traces; the paper does not describe a systematic, reproducible annotation protocol (e.g., rubric, multiple annotators, agreement statistics) for attributing errors to panic vs. self-doubt vs. other causes.

The mitigation ('prompt guidance' injected in the model's own voice asserting the update is verified and correct) is somewhat artificial: it sidesteps the realistic scenario where the model must decide whether to trust an update, so the claim that guidance 'fully resolves' self-doubt on GSM8K/MATH500 has limited practical significance.

Novelty is moderate: the hard-interrupt setting overlaps substantially with budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025) and the update-driven setting with Fan et al. (2025); the paper's differentiation is articulated but the core contribution is primarily a re-scoping of known phenomena into an interactive setting plus a new dataset, rather than new understanding of mechanism.

Several results (early interruption lowers accuracy; speedup instructions shorten outputs but can hurt hard tasks) are somewhat expected and the analysis largely describes rather than explains the failure modes; no investigation of why leakage or panic occurs (e.g., token-level analysis, training-data effects beyond the single EOS observation for Qwen3-1.7B).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant question: LRM robustness when the 'frozen world' assumption breaks down (mid-inference interruptions and context updates). The problem framing via a two-stage formalization M(q)→(r_x, x) and M(q, r_x, x, i)→(r'_x, a') is clean and general.

The taxonomy of three failure modes — reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt — is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution, and is supported with concrete qualitative examples (Listing C.1, C.2, C.3, Figure 5) rather than only aggregate statistics.

The evaluation covers two complementary intervention types (hard/soft time-constrained and update-driven), multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, LiveCodeBench-v6), and includes a model-scaling ablation (Qwen3 1.7B/8B/32B) plus an assistant-turn vs. user-turn comparison (Figure 8).

The update-driven dataset is constructed with a multi-stage pipeline (decomposition, augmentation, manual verification) and the appendix discloses prompts and LLM usage, which aids reproducibility. Code, data, and a project page are promised.
The limitations section (Section 7) is honest about the narrow task domains, single well-defined interruptions, and the small model set.
weaknesses: Limited scope of evidence for headline claims: only three open-weight models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magstral-S1.2-24B) are tested, all small-to-mid scale. No frontier or closed models are evaluated, so claims that 'static evaluations consistently overestimate robustness' of state-of-the-art LRMs are weakly supported. Many headline numbers ('up to 60% drop', '10x longer answers', 'over 90% of panic errors') appear to be worst-case picks across interrupt positions, models, and tasks.

Many findings are fairly predictable/intuitive: interrupting earlier yields worse answers; models comply with speedup requests; late updates are hard to incorporate. The closest prior work (s1 budget forcing, Muiennighoff et al. 2025; missing-premise overthinking, Fan et al. 2025) already covers much of this territory; the paper's differentiation (interactive, externally imposed cutoffs) is real but the incremental novelty of the empirical conclusions is modest.

The main experimental design uses assistant-turn interruptions — injecting tokens directly into the ongoing reasoning trace — which is an artificial intervention mode that most deployed systems cannot actually perform. The more realistic user-turn setting is relegated to an ablation and is confounded by the authors' own admission that Qwen3 and Magstral 'struggle with consistent formatting' under it, leaving the central conclusions tied to the less realistic setup.

The 'prompt guidance' mitigation is ad hoc and its success is unsurprising: the guidance tells the model the update 'is correct and verified by the user,' which effectively resolves self-doubt by fiat rather than by improving genuine update-integration ability. No stronger baselines (e.g., re-reading instructions, chain-of-thought restart prompts) are compared, and no ablation isolates which part of the guidance template matters.

The error-mode quantification methodology is under-specified: how 'doubt rate' and 'panic rate' are measured or classified (e.g., '80% of update-driven errors stem from self-doubt') is not clearly defined, and appears to rely on qualitative judgment that could be subjective. No inter-annotator agreement or automated classifier validation is reported for the dataset or the failure-mode labels.

Dataset construction details are thin in key respects: the size of the update-driven dataset is not clearly stated, there is no contamination analysis despite the augmented problems being derived from widely memorized benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME), and correctness of augmented ground-truth answers for coding tasks (against hidden tests) is not rigorously validated.

Statistical rigor is uneven: 16 trials for AIME but single runs elsewhere; bootstrap CIs on plots are shown but many claimed differences (e.g., soft vs. hard interrupt effects, scale trends) are small relative to the visible variance bands.

Presentation issues: Figure 1b's stacked-bar encoding of total vs. panic/doubt error rates is hard to read, legends in Figures 2 and 6 are cluttered, and the paper sometimes reports conclusions in prose that are difficult to trace to specific figures (e.g., the '80%' self-doubt attribution).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether Large Reasoning Models remain robust when their inference is interrupted mid-thought or when the problem specification changes during reasoning. The framing against the 'frozen world' assumption is well motivated and connects to realistic deployment scenarios (assistants, coding agents) that prior efficient-reasoning work largely ignores.

The formal setup (Section 3.1) is clean: decomposing inference into two stages with an interruption condition, and defining interruption-conditioned accuracy and post-interruption output length, gives the study a precise, reusable evaluation protocol rather than a collection of ad hoc anecdotes.

The taxonomy of failure modes — reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt — is a genuinely interesting empirical contribution. The qualitative examples in Appendix C (e.g., the leaked chain-of-thought embedded in code comments, and the self-doubt loop) are convincing and illustrate phenomena that static evaluations would never surface.

Dataset construction is documented in reasonable detail (Appendix D): updates are designed to be semantically required (a*(q) != a*(q,u)), generated with GPT-5 and manually verified, with multiple worked examples across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and coding tasks, including both necessary and helpful updates.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: full system and injection prompts are provided in Appendix B, hyperparameters follow official model cards, the vLLM framework is specified, and Project Page / Code / Dataset links are included. AIME's high variance is handled with 16 trials following the DeepSeek-R1 protocol and bootstrapped CIs.

Useful ablations beyond the main claims: model scaling (1.7B/8B/32B) revealing that interruptibility itself does not simply scale, assistant-turn vs. user-turn interruption placement, and a speedup-augmented update condition. The limitations section is honest about domain coverage (math/coding only), single well-defined interventions, and the small model set.

The paper positions itself carefully against related work (s1 budget forcing, NoThinking, TALE, Fan et al. on missing premises), articulating a distinct contribution: externally imposed, unpredictable interruptions with content updates rather than pre-fixed budgets.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claims rest on a narrow experimental base: only three small-to-mid-size open models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-1.2). There is no evidence about whether the reported failures (panic, self-doubt, up-to-60% degradation) persist for frontier or larger models, which limits the practical significance of the 'static evaluations overestimate robustness' headline claim.

Single runs are used for most datasets (only AIME gets 16 trials). For GSM8K (near ceiling) and MATH500, accuracy differences of a few points under interruption may be within sampling noise, and per-datapoint AIME (30 problems) is small; the paper would be more convincing with multi-trial evaluation throughout or explicit per-item analysis.

There is a potential confound in the update-driven setting: some augmented problems are not merely the original problem with an update, but substantially harder instances (e.g., the AIME example changes an 8x8 grid/length-16 path problem into an 18x18 grid/length-36 problem). Degradation under late updates may partly reflect intrinsic difficulty of the augmented problem rather than the model's failure to integrate the update. A control comparing full-thinking accuracy on augmented problems vs. interrupted accuracy is needed to isolate the effect.

Ground-truth answers for augmented coding problems rely on GPT-5-generated changes plus author verification; the paper does not describe executing or validating reference solutions against test cases for all augmented tasks, leaving some risk of label noise in the coding results.

The prompt-guidance mitigation is ad hoc (injecting 'the update is verified' in the model's voice) and its mechanism is not analyzed; it improves results but the paper does not disentangle whether it fixes self-doubt or simply forces unconditional acceptance of updates, which could be harmful if updates were wrong. This borders on training the eval into the prompt rather than understanding the failure.

Several findings partially restate known results: budget-forcing overthinking (Muennighoff et al.), degradation under reasoning removal (NoThinking, Wang et al.), and longer output under problematic premises (Fan et al.). The genuinely new elements are the update-driven setting and the named pathologies, but the headline 'up to 60%' statistic conflates phenomena with differing novelty.

Presentation issues: Figure 1(b) and several main-text plots are dense and hard to parse at print resolution; some claims in the abstract (e.g., 'over 90% of new errors under speedup arise from panic') are not traceable to a clearly labeled table in the main text and require cross-referencing figures.

The 'assistant-turn' interruption method (injecting text directly into the reasoning trace) is a specific implementation choice justified partly by Qwen3's format constraints; results under this scheme may not transfer to how real products expose interruption, and the user-turn comparison (Section 6.2) is relegated to an ablation despite being arguably the more realistic setting.
